stem: A 45-year-old woman who recently immigrated to the United States is hospitalized due to exertional dyspnea and fatigue.  She has no significant medical history and takes no medications.  Blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg and pulse is 90/min and regular.  After cardiopulmonary examination, the physician suspects mitral stenosis.  Which of the following parameters is the most useful measure for assessing the degree of stenosis?​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌
explanation:
On auscultation, the best indicator of mitral stenosis severity is the length of time between S2 (specifically the A2 component, caused by aortic valve closure) and the opening snap (OS).  The OS occurs due to abrupt tensing of the valve leaflets as the mitral valve reaches its maximum diameter during forceful opening.

As the severity of mitral stenosis worsens, left atrial pressure increases due to impaired passage of blood through the valve into the left ventricle.  Higher left atrial pressure causes the valve to open earlier in diastole because the pressure threshold to open the valve is reached more quickly.  Therefore, a relatively shorter A2-to-OS interval correlates with more severe mitral stenosis.

Mitral stenosis severity can be confirmed by measuring the mean transvalvular pressure gradient via Doppler echocardiography.

(Choices B and C)  Left-sided S3 and S4 gallops are generally absent in mitral stenosis because left ventricular filling is normal or decreased.  When mitral stenosis is severe enough to cause pulmonary hypertension, patients may develop right-sided heart failure, and a right-sided S3 and/or S4 can occur.  However, these right-sided gallops arise only in severe, end-stage mitral stenosis and are otherwise not useful for differentiating stenosis severity (eg, distinguishing between mild or moderate disease).

(Choice D)  Diastolic rumble intensity in mitral stenosis does not correlate well with stenosis severity.  This is due to murmur intensity being dependent on both the transvalvular pressure gradient and the amount of blood flowing through the valve.  In very severe stenosis, the diastolic murmur may be absent due to greatly reduced flow across the valve.

(Choice E)  Presystolic accentuation of the mitral stenosis murmur occurs due to increased transvalvular flow driven by left atrial contraction.  This accentuation is heard across a wide range of mitral stenosis severity.  If mitral stenosis precipitates atrial fibrillation (due to left atrial enlargement), organized atrial contraction is lost and presystolic accentuation of the murmur disappears.

Educational objective:The best and most reliable auscultatory indicator of mitral stenosis severity is the A2-to-opening snap interval; a relatively shorter interval indicates more severe stenosis.  Other auscultatory findings include a diastolic rumbling murmur with presystolic accentuation.​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌
